Turkish Lira Crisis of 2021 Disrupted Industry, Hit Ford Otomotiv Sanayi AS

ISTANBUL, June 7 — The sharp depreciation of the Turkish lira during the 2021 currency crisis caused wide-ranging disruptions across Turkey’s economy, with leading manufacturers such as Ford Otomotiv Sanayi AS forced to scale back operations amid soaring costs and supply chain turmoil.

The crisis, which began in late 2021, saw the lira lose nearly 45% of its value against the US dollar in the space of a few months, triggering a spike in inflation and undermining business confidence throughout the country. The Turkish Statistical Institute reported that annual consumer inflation reached 36% by December 2021, the highest level in two decades.

Ford Otomotiv Sanayi AS, one of Turkey’s largest automotive producers, faced “unprecedented challenges” as the lira’s decline drove up the cost of imported components, a company spokesperson said at the time. “Logistical bottlenecks and foreign exchange volatility forced us to temporarily reduce production and revise our export plans,” the spokesperson added.

Trade groups said the crisis reverberated through all major sectors, with the Turkish Exporters Assembly noting a sharp fall in export profits despite strong overseas demand. “The currency collapse created a paradox for exporters — higher competitiveness abroad, but shrinking margins at home due to rising input costs,” said assembly chairman Ismail Cevik.

The lira’s fall also strained the country’s banking sector, as borrowers struggled to service foreign currency-denominated debts. The Confederation of Progressive Trade Unions warned in January 2022 that “workers faced real wage losses and job insecurity as companies responded to the crisis with layoffs and furloughs.”

The government announced a series of emergency measures, including state-backed currency protection schemes and interventions in foreign exchange markets, in an effort to stabilize the situation. Analysts say these actions helped curb the worst effects, and Turkey’s industrial activity has since returned to pre-crisis levels.

Economist Ece Demir of the Istanbul Policy Center said, “The 2021 currency crisis was a wake-up call for the Turkish economy. While the acute disruption has passed, companies remain cautious about future volatility.”
